{{short description|Theory of gravity}}
{{Technical|date=July 2019}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:<var>f</var>(<var>R</var>) gravity}}

In [[physics]], '''''f''(''R'')''' is a type of [[Alternatives to general relativity|modified gravity]] theory which generalizes [[Albert Einstein|Einstein's]] [[general relativity]]. ''f''(''R'') gravity is actually a family of theories, each one defined by a different function, {{var|f}}, of the [[Scalar curvature|Ricci scalar]], {{var|R}}. The simplest case is just the function being equal to the scalar; this is general relativity. As a consequence of introducing an arbitrary function, there may be freedom to explain the [[Accelerating universe|accelerated expansion]] and [[structure formation]] of the Universe without adding unknown forms of [[dark energy]] or [[dark matter]]. Some functional forms may be inspired by corrections arising from a [[Quantum gravity|quantum theory of gravity]]. ''f''(''R'') gravity was first proposed in 1970 by [[Hans Adolph Buchdahl]]<ref>{{cite journal| title = Non-linear Lagrangians and cosmological theory| last=Buchdahl |first=H. A.| journal = [[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]]| volume = 150| pages = 1–8| year = 1970| bibcode = 1970MNRAS.150....1B| doi=10.1093/mnras/150.1.1| doi-access = free}}</ref> (although {{var|ϕ}} was used rather than {{var|f}} for the name of the arbitrary function). It has become an active field of research following work by [[Alexei Starobinsky]] on [[Inflation (cosmology)|cosmic inflation]].<ref>{{cite journal| title = A new type of isotropic cosmological models without singularity| last=Starobinsky |first=A. A.| journal = [[Physics Letters B]] | volume = 91| pages = 99–102| year = 1980| issue=1 |doi = 10.1016/0370-2693(80)90670-X| bibcode = 1980PhLB...91...99S }}</ref> A wide range of phenomena can be produced from this theory by adopting different functions; however, many functional forms can now be ruled out on observational grounds, or because of pathological theoretical problems.

== Introduction ==

In ''f''(''R'') gravity, one seeks to generalize the [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] of the [[Einstein–Hilbert action]]:
<math display="block">S[g]= \int {1 \over 2\kappa} R \sqrt{-g} \, \mathrm{d}^4x </math>
to
<math display="block">S[g]= \int {1 \over 2\kappa} f(R) \sqrt{-g} \, \mathrm{d}^4x </math>
where <math>\kappa=\tfrac{8\pi G}{c^4}, g = \det g_{\mu\nu}</math> is the determinant of the [[metric tensor]], and ''f''(''R'') is some function of the [[scalar curvature|Ricci scalar]].<ref name="DE textbook Amendola-Tsujikawa"> [https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/dark-energy/EC55E8BF946C34D61B758273D8286618 L. Amendola and S. Tsujikawa (2013) "Dark Energy, Theory and Observations"] Cambridge University Press</ref>

There are two ways to track the effect of changing ''R'' to ''f''(''R''), i.e., to obtain the theory [[field equation]]s. The first is to use [[#Metric_f(R)_gravity|metric formalism]] and the second is to use the [[#Palatini_f(R)_gravity|Palatini formalism]].<ref name="DE textbook Amendola-Tsujikawa" /> While the two formalisms lead to the same field equations for General Relativity, i.e., when ''f''(''R'') = ''R'', the field equations may differ when ''f''(''R'') ≠ ''R''.

== Metric ''f''(''R'') gravity ==

=== Derivation of field equations ===
In metric ''f''(''R'') gravity, one arrives at the field equations by varying the action with respect to the [[Metric_tensor_(general_relativity)|metric]] and not treating the [[Mathematics_of_general_relativity#Affine_connections|connection]] <math>\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}</math> independently. For completeness we will now briefly mention the basic steps of the variation of the action. The main steps are the same as in the case of the variation of the [[Einstein–Hilbert action]] (see the article for more details) but there are also some important differences.

The variation of the determinant is as always:
<math display="block">\delta \sqrt{-g}= -\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{-g} g_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu}</math>

The [[Ricci scalar]] is defined as
<math display="block"> R = g^{\mu\nu} R_{\mu\nu}.</math>

Therefore, its variation with respect to the inverse metric <math>g^{\mu\nu}</math> is given by
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\delta R &= R_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu} + g^{\mu\nu} \delta R_{\mu\nu}\\
 &= R_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu} + g^{\mu\nu} \left (\nabla_\rho \delta \Gamma^\rho_{\nu\mu} - \nabla_\nu \delta \Gamma^\rho_{\rho\mu} \right )
\end{align}</math>

For the second step see the article about the [[Einstein–Hilbert action]]. Since <math>\delta\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}</math> is the difference of two connections, it should transform as a tensor. Therefore, it can be written as 
<math display="block">\delta \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{2}g^{\lambda a}\left(\nabla_\mu\delta g_{a\nu}+\nabla_\nu\delta g_{a\mu}-\nabla_a\delta g_{\mu\nu} \right).</math>

Substituting into the equation above:
<math display="block">\delta R= R_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu}+g_{\mu\nu}\Box \delta g^{\mu\nu}-\nabla_\mu \nabla_\nu \delta g^{\mu\nu}</math>
where <math>\nabla_\mu</math> is the [[covariant derivative]] and <math>\square = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\nabla_\nu</math> is the [[d'Alembert operator]].

Denoting <math>F(R) = \frac{df}{d R}</math>, the variation in the action reads:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\delta S[g]&= \int \frac{1}{2\kappa} \left(\delta f(R) \sqrt{-g}+f(R) \delta \sqrt{-g} \right)\, \mathrm{d}^4x \\
 &= \int \frac{1}{2\kappa} \left(F(R) \delta R \sqrt{-g}-\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{-g} g_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu} f(R)\right) \, \mathrm{d}^4x \\
 &= \int \frac{1}{2\kappa} \sqrt{-g}\left(F(R)(R_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu}+g_{\mu\nu}\Box \delta g^{\mu\nu}-\nabla_\mu \nabla_\nu \delta g^{\mu\nu}) -\frac{1}{2} g_{\mu\nu} \delta g^{\mu\nu} f(R) \right)\, \mathrm{d}^4x 
\end{align}</math>

Doing [[integration by parts]] on the second and third terms (and neglected the boundary contributions), we get:
<math display="block">\delta S[g]= \int \frac{1}{2\kappa} \sqrt{-g}\delta g^{\mu\nu} \left(F(R)R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu} f(R)+[g_{\mu\nu}\Box -\nabla_\mu \nabla_\nu]F(R) \right)\, \mathrm{d}^4x.</math>

By demanding that the action remains invariant under variations of the metric, <math>\frac{\delta S}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}=0</math>, one obtains the field equations:
<math display="block">F(R)R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}f(R)+\left[ g_{\mu\nu} \Box-\nabla_\mu \nabla_\nu \right]F(R) = \kappa T_{\mu\nu},</math>
where <math>T_{\mu\nu}</math> is the [[energy–momentum tensor]] defined as
<math display="block">T_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta(\sqrt{-g} \mathcal L_\mathrm{m})}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}},</math>
where <math>\mathcal L_m</math> is the matter Lagrangian.

=== Generalized Friedmann equations ===
Assuming a [[Robertson–Walker metric]] with scale factor <math>a(t)</math> we can find the generalized [[Friedmann equations]] to be (in units where <math>\kappa = 1</math>):
<math display="block">  3F H^{2} = \rho_{{\rm m}}+\rho_{{\rm rad}}+\frac{1}{2}(FR-f)-3H{\dot F}</math>
<math display="block">-2F\dot{H} = \rho_{{\rm m}}+\frac{4}{3}\rho_{{\rm rad}}+\ddot{F}-H\dot{F},</math>
where
<math display="block">H = \frac{\dot{a}}{a}</math> is the [[Hubble parameter]], 
the dot is the derivative with respect to the cosmic time {{var|t}}, and the terms {{var|ρ}}<sub>m</sub> and {{var|ρ}}<sub>rad</sub> represent the matter and radiation densities respectively; these satisfy the [[continuity equation]]s:
<math display="block"> \dot{\rho}_{{\rm m}}+3H\rho_{{\rm m}}=0;</math>
<math display="block"> \dot{\rho}_{{\rm rad}}+4H\rho_{{\rm rad}}=0.</math>

=== Modified gravitational constant ===
An interesting feature of these theories is the fact that the [[gravitational constant]] is time and scale dependent.<ref>{{cite journal| last1= Tsujikawa |first1=Shinji|title=Matter density perturbations and effective gravitational constant in modified gravity models of dark energy| journal =Physical Review D|date=2007|volume=76|issue=2|article-number=023514|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.76.023514 |arxiv=0705.1032|bibcode=2007PhRvD..76b3514T|s2cid=119324187}}</ref> To see this, add a small scalar perturbation to the metric (in the [[Newtonian gauge]]):
<math display="block">\mathrm{d}s^2 = -(1+2\Phi)\mathrm{d}t^2 +\alpha^2 (1-2\Psi)\delta_{ij}\mathrm{d}x^i \mathrm{d}x^j</math>
where {{varserif|Φ}} and {{varserif|Ψ}} are the Newtonian potentials and use the field equations to first order. After some lengthy calculations, one can define a [[Poisson equation]] in the Fourier space and attribute the extra terms that appear on the right-hand side to an effective gravitational constant {{var|G}}<sub>eff</sub>. Doing so, we get the gravitational potential (valid on sub-[[Cosmological_horizon|horizon]] scales {{nowrap|1={{var|k}}<sup>2</sup> ≫ {{var|a}}<sup>2</sup>{{var|H}}<sup>2</sup>}}):
<math display="block">\Phi = -4\pi G_\mathrm{eff} \frac{a^2}{k^2} \delta\rho_\mathrm{m} </math>
where {{var|δ}}{{var|ρ}}<sub>m</sub> is a perturbation in the matter density, {{var|k}} is the Fourier scale and {{var|G}}<sub>eff</sub> is:
<math display="block"> G_\mathrm{eff}=\frac{1}{8\pi F}\frac{1+4\frac{k^2}{a^2R}m}{1+3\frac{k^2}{a^2R}m},</math>
with
<math display="block"> m\equiv\frac{RF_{,R}}{F}.</math>

=== Massive gravitational waves ===

This class of theories when linearized exhibits three polarization modes for the [[gravitational wave]]s, of which two correspond to the massless [[graviton]] (helicities ±2) and the third (scalar) is coming from the fact that if we take into account a conformal transformation, the fourth order theory {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) becomes [[general relativity]] plus a [[scalar field]]. To see this, identify
<math display="block"> \Phi \to f'(R) \quad \textrm{and} \quad \frac{dV}{d\Phi}\to\frac{2f(R)-R f'(R)}{3},</math>
and use the field equations above to get
<math display="block">\Box \Phi=\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}\Phi}</math>

Working to first order of perturbation theory:
<math display="block"> g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+h_{\mu\nu} </math>
<math display="block"> \Phi=\Phi_0+\delta \Phi</math>
and after some tedious algebra, one can solve for the metric perturbation, which corresponds to the gravitational waves. A particular frequency component, for a wave propagating in the {{var|z}}-direction, may be written as
<math display="block">h_{\mu\nu}(t,z;\omega)=A^{+}(\omega)\exp(-i\omega(t-z))e^{+}_{\mu\nu}+A^{\times}(\omega)\exp(-i\omega(t-z))e^{\times}_{\mu\nu} +h_f(v_\mathrm{g} t-z;\omega) \eta_{\mu\nu} </math>
where
<math display="block"> h_f\equiv \frac{\delta \Phi}{\Phi_0},</math>
and {{var|v}}<sub>g</sub>({{var|ω}})&nbsp;=&nbsp;d{{var|ω}}/d{{var|k}} is the [[group velocity]] of a [[wave packet]] {{var|h}}<sub>{{var|f}}</sub> centred on wave-vector {{var|k}}. The first two terms correspond to the usual [[Gravitational waves#Linear approximation|transverse polarizations]] from general relativity, while the third corresponds to the new massive polarization mode of {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) theories. This mode is a mixture of massless transverse breathing mode (but not traceless) and massive longitudinal scalar mode.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.95.104034 |title=Polarizations of gravitational waves in ''f''(''R'') gravity |journal=Phys. Rev. D  |volume=95 |article-number=104034 |year=2017 | last1=Liang | first1=Dicong | last2=Gong |first2= Yungui | last3=Hou |first3= Shaoqi | last4=Liu |first4= Yunqi |issue=10 |arxiv=1701.05998 |bibcode=2017PhRvD..95j4034L |s2cid=119005163 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-020-08684-3  |doi-access=free|title=A new f(R) gravity model and properties of gravitational waves in it |journal=The European Physical Journal C  |volume=80 |page=1101 |year=2020 | last1=Gogoi | first1=Dhruba Jyoti | last2=Dev Goswami |first2= Umananda |issue=12 |arxiv= 2006.04011 |bibcode=2020EPJC...80.1101G |s2cid=219530929 }}</ref> The transverse and traceless modes (also known as tensor modes) propagate at the [[speed of light]], but the massive scalar mode moves at a speed {{var|v}}<sub>G</sub>&nbsp;<&nbsp;1 (in units where {{var|c}}&nbsp;=&nbsp;1), this mode is dispersive. However, in {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) gravity metric formalism, for the model <math> f(R) = \alpha R^2 </math> (also known as pure <math> R^2 </math> model), the third polarization mode is a pure breathing mode and propagate with the speed of light through the spacetime.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s12648-020-01998-8 |title=Gravitational Waves in f(R) Gravity Power Law Model |journal=Indian Journal of Physics |year=2022 | last1=Gogoi | first1=Dhruba Jyoti | last2=Dev Goswami |first2= Umananda |volume=96 |issue=2 |page=637 |arxiv= 1901.11277 |bibcode=2022InJPh..96..637G |s2cid=231655238 }}</ref>

== Equivalent formalism ==

Under certain additional conditions<ref>{{cite journal|last1=De Felice|first1=Antonio|last2=Tsujikawa|first2=Shinji|title=f(R) Theories|journal=Living Reviews in Relativity|date=2010|volume=13|issue=1|page=3|doi=10.12942/lrr-2010-3|doi-access=free |pmid=28179828|pmc=5255939|arxiv=1002.4928|bibcode=2010LRR....13....3D}}</ref> we can simplify the analysis of {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) theories by introducing an [[auxiliary field]] {{varserif|Φ}}. Assuming <math>f''(R) \neq 0</math> for all {{var|R}}, let {{var|V}}({{var|Φ}}) be the [[Legendre transformation]] of {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) so that <math>\Phi = f'(R)</math> and <math>R=V'(\Phi)</math>. Then, one obtains the O'Hanlon (1972) action:
<math display="block">S = \int d^4x \sqrt{-g} \left[ \frac{1}{2\kappa}\left(\Phi R - V(\Phi)\right) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{m}}\right].</math>

We have the [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler–Lagrange equations]]:
<math display="block">V'(\Phi)=R</math>
<math display="block">\Phi \left( R_{\mu\nu} - \frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu} R \right) + \left(g_{\mu\nu}\Box -\nabla_\mu \nabla_\nu \right) \Phi + \frac{1}{2} g_{\mu\nu}V(\Phi) = \kappa T_{\mu\nu}</math>

Eliminating {{varserif|Φ}}, we obtain exactly the same equations as before. However, the equations are only second order in the derivatives, instead of fourth order.

We are currently working with the [[Jordan and Einstein frames|Jordan frame]]. By performing a conformal rescaling:
<math display="block">\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu}=\Phi g_{\mu\nu},</math>
we transform to the [[Einstein frame]]:
<math display="block">R = \Phi \left[ \tilde{R} + \frac{3\tilde{\Box} \Phi}{\Phi} -\frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\tilde{\nabla} \Phi}{\Phi}\right)^2 \right]</math>
<math display="block">S = \int d^4x \sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\frac{1}{2\kappa}\left[ \tilde{R} - \frac{3}{2}\left( \frac{\tilde{\nabla}\Phi}{\Phi} \right)^2 - \frac{V(\Phi)}{\Phi^2} \right]</math>
after integrating by parts.

Defining <math>\tilde{\Phi} = \sqrt{3} \ln{\Phi}</math>, and substituting
<math display="block">S = \int \mathrm{d}^4x \sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\frac{1}{2\kappa}\left[ \tilde{R} - \frac{1}{2}\left(\tilde{\nabla}\tilde{\Phi}\right)^2 - \tilde{V}(\tilde{\Phi}) \right]</math>
<math display="block">\tilde{V}(\tilde{\Phi}) = e^{-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \tilde{\Phi}} V \left (e^{\tilde{\Phi}/\sqrt{3}} \right ).</math>

This is general relativity coupled to a real scalar field: using ''f''(''R'') theories to describe the accelerating universe is practically equivalent to using [[quintessence (physics)|quintessence]]. (At least, equivalent up to the caveat that we have not yet specified matter couplings, so (for example) ''f''(''R'') gravity in which matter is minimally coupled to the metric (i.e., in Jordan frame) is equivalent to a quintessence theory in which the scalar field mediates a fifth force with gravitational strength.)

== Palatini ''f''(''R'') gravity ==

In [[Palatini variation|Palatini]] ''f''(''R'') gravity, one treats the metric and [[Connection (mathematics)|connection]] independently and varies the action with respect to each of them separately. The matter Lagrangian is assumed to be independent of the connection. These theories have been shown to be equivalent to [[Brans–Dicke theory]] with {{nowrap|1={{var|ω}} = &minus;{{frac|3|2}}}}.<ref name="flanagan04">{{cite journal| title = The conformal frame freedom in theories of gravitation| last= Flanagan |first=E. E.| journal = [[Classical and Quantum Gravity]] | volume = 21| pages = 3817–3829| year = 2004| doi = 10.1088/0264-9381/21/15/N02 | bibcode = 2004CQGra..21.3817F |arxiv = gr-qc/0403063| issue = 15 | s2cid= 117619981 }}</ref><ref name="olmo05">{{cite journal| title = The Gravity Lagrangian According to Solar System Experiments| last= Olmo |first=G. J.| journal = [[Physical Review Letters]] | volume = 95| article-number = 261102| year = 2005| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.261102 | bibcode = 2005PhRvL..95z1102O |arxiv = gr-qc/0505101| issue = 26| pmid = 16486333 | s2cid= 27440524 }}</ref> Due to the structure of the theory, however, Palatini {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) theories appear to be in conflict with the Standard Model,<ref name="flanagan04"/><ref>{{cite journal| title =How (not) to use the Palatini formulation of scalar-tensor gravity| last1= Iglesias |first1=A. |last2=Kaloper |first2=N. |last3=Padilla |first3=A. |last4=Park |first4=M.| journal = [[Physical Review D]] | volume = 76| article-number = 104001| year = 2007| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.76.104001 | bibcode = 2007PhRvD..76j4001I |arxiv = 0708.1163| issue =10 }}</ref> may violate Solar system experiments,<ref name="olmo05"/> and seem to create unwanted singularities.<ref>{{cite journal| title =A no-go theorem for polytropic spheres in Palatini ''f''(''R'') gravity| last1=Barausse |first1=E. |last2=Sotiriou |first2=T. P. |last3=Miller |first3=J. C.| journal = [[Classical and Quantum Gravity]] | volume = 25| article-number = 062001| year = 2008| doi = 10.1088/0264-9381/25/6/062001 | bibcode = 2008CQGra..25f2001B |arxiv = gr-qc/0703132| issue =6 | s2cid=119370540 }}</ref>

== Metric-affine ''f''(''R'') gravity ==

In [[Metric-affine gravitation theory|metric-affine]] ''f''(''R'') gravity, one generalizes things even further, treating both the metric and connection independently, and assuming the matter Lagrangian depends on the connection as well.

== Observational tests ==

As there are many potential forms of ''f''(''R'') gravity, it is difficult to find generic tests. Additionally, since deviations away from General Relativity can be made arbitrarily small in some cases, it is impossible to conclusively exclude some modifications. Some progress can be made, without assuming a concrete form for the function ''f''(''R'') by [[Taylor series|Taylor expanding]]
<math display="block">f(R) = a_0 + a_1 R + a_2 R^2 + \cdots</math>

The first term is like the [[cosmological constant]] and must be small. The next coefficient {{var|a}}<sub>1</sub> can be set to one as in general relativity. For metric ''f''(''R'') gravity (as opposed to Palatini or metric-affine {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) gravity), the quadratic term is best constrained by [[fifth force]] measurements, since it leads to a [[Yukawa potential|Yukawa]] correction to the gravitational potential. The best current bounds are {{nowrap|{{abs|{{var|a}}<sub>2</sub>}} < {{val|4|e=−9|u=m2}}}} or equivalently {{nowrap|{{abs|{{var|a}}<sub>2</sub>}} < {{val|2.3|e=22|u=GeV<sup>−2</sup>}}.}}<ref name="Berry">{{cite journal| title = Linearized ''f''(''R'') gravity: Gravitational radiation and Solar System tests| last1= Berry |first1=C. P. L. |last2= Gair |first2=J. R.| journal = [[Physical Review D]] | volume = 83| article-number = 104022| year = 2011| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.83.104022| bibcode = 2011PhRvD..83j4022B |arxiv = 1104.0819| issue = 10 | s2cid= 119202399 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| title = Dark Matter from R<sup>2</sup> Gravity| last1=Cembranos |first1=J. A. R.| journal = [[Physical Review Letters]] | volume = 102| article-number = 141301| year = 2009| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.141301| bibcode = 2009PhRvL.102n1301C |arxiv = 0809.1653| issue = 14| pmid = 19392422 | s2cid=33042847 }}</ref>

The [[parameterized post-Newtonian formalism]] is designed to be able to constrain generic modified theories of gravity. However, {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) gravity shares many of the same values as General Relativity, and is therefore indistinguishable using these tests.<ref>{{cite journal| title = Parametrized post-Newtonian limit of fourth-order theories of gravity| last1= Clifton |first1=T.| journal = [[Physical Review D]] | volume = 77| article-number = 024041 | year = 2008| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.77.024041| bibcode = 2008PhRvD..77b4041C |arxiv = 0801.0983| issue = 2 | s2cid= 54174617 }}</ref> In particular light deflection is unchanged, so {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) gravity, like General Relativity, is entirely consistent with the bounds from [[Cassini–Huygens#Tests of general relativity|Cassini tracking]].<ref name="Berry" />

== Starobinsky gravity ==
{{main|Starobinsky inflation}}
Starobinsky gravity has the following form
<math display="block"> f(R) = R + \frac{R^2}{6M^2}</math>
where <math>M</math> has the dimensions of mass.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(80)90670-X |title=A new type of isotropic cosmological models without singularity |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=91 |pages=99–102 |year=1980 |last1=Starobinsky |first1=A.A |issue=1 |bibcode=1980PhLB...91...99S }}</ref>

Starobinsky gravity provides a mechanism for the cosmic [[Inflation_(cosmology)|inflation]], just after the [[Big Bang]] when ''R'' was still large. However, it is not suited to describe the present [[Accelerating expansion of the universe|universe acceleration]] since at present ''R'' is very small.<ref name="NASA_Shape">{{cite web |title=Will the Universe expand forever? |url=http://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/uni_shape.html |publisher=[[NASA]] |date=24 January 2014 |access-date=16 March 2015}}</ref><ref name="Fermi_Flat">{{cite web |title=Our universe is Flat|url= http://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/april-2015/our-flat-universe?email_issue=725 |publisher=FermiLab/SLAC |date=7 April 2015 |first = Lauren|last = Biron|work = symmetrymagazine.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Unexpected connections|author=Marcus Y. Yoo|journal=Engineering & Science|volume=LXXIV1|date=2011|page=30}}</ref> This implies that the quadratic term in <math>f(R) = R + \frac{R^2}{6M^2}</math> is negligible, i.e., one tends to ''f''(''R'') = ''R'' which is general relativity with a zero [[cosmological constant]].

== Gogoi–Goswami gravity ==
Gogoi–Goswami gravity (named after Dhruba Jyoti Gogoi and Umananda Dev Goswami) has the following form
<math display="block"> f(R) = R - \frac{\alpha}{\pi} R_c \cot^{-1} \left( \frac{R_c^2}{R^2} \right) - \beta R_c \left[ 1 - \exp\left( - \frac{R}{R_c} \right) \right] </math>
where <math> \alpha </math> and <math> \beta </math> are two dimensionless positive constants and ''R''<sub>c</sub> is a characteristic curvature constant.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-020-08684-3  |doi-access=free|title=A new f(R) gravity model and properties of gravitational waves in it |journal=The European Physical Journal C  |volume=80 |page=1101 |year=2020 | last1=Gogoi | first1=Dhruba Jyoti | last2=Dev Goswami |first2= Umananda |issue=12 |arxiv= 2006.04011 |bibcode=2020EPJC...80.1101G |s2cid=219530929 }}</ref>

== Tensorial generalization ==

''f''(''R'') gravity as presented in the previous sections is a scalar modification of general relativity. More generally, we can have a 
<math display="block">\int \mathrm{d}^Dx \sqrt{-g}\, f(R, R^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}, R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma})</math>
coupling involving invariants of the [[Ricci tensor]] and the [[Weyl tensor]]. Special cases are {{var|f}}({{var|R}}) gravity, [[conformal gravity]], [[Gauss–Bonnet gravity]] and [[Lovelock gravity]]. Notice that with any nontrivial tensorial dependence, we typically have additional massive spin-2 degrees of freedom, in addition to the massless graviton and a massive scalar. An exception is Gauss–Bonnet gravity where the fourth order terms for the spin-2 components cancel out.
